title: Birth date, family instruments and first guitar
summary: Born 1889; parents played nothing; Freddie began on violin and mandolin, Louis thumped a boxwood guitar and they played for friends as small boys. Talk of his ailing sister.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: You might give your birth date if you don't mind.
Well, born February the 2nd, 1889. And may I ask you a question, Mr. Certainly. Well, I want to find out, do you want to find out about bands and different things right now?

Yes. Anything, it doesn't have to be in any special order, but just anything that you happen to think of. We might ask a little bit more about your family. Did your father or mother play any instruments? No, they're nothing whatever.
They just brought us up. The first thing we started on, he started on a violin. I believe I gave it to you, Mr. Yes. We have the mandolin.

The mandolin. And he had a violin, but of course by me he left him to lay up and lay up and it just went to the jump power. Which did he start on, the violin or the mandolin? The violin first and then after the mandolin. Then he started with the card game. Then he played harmonica. When he was playing harmonica, then the last thing he picked up was the violin and I had a guitar with my mother and father. I was like a guitar, you know, I can't hear me. It wasn't a guitar exactly, but it was made out of old boxwood. And well I must have been about, say about seven, eight years old. And she used to bring us around different corners to our friends. And Freddie used to have his violin, I had an old guitar, just hit and didn't know what I was doing or whatever. I was just thumping on it and didn't know if it was B-flap to G or F or C or nothing. I just hit on it. Well of course the people had liked us because we were so young to be going around and we used to take and talk. How old were you then? Well I must have been about nine years old and he must have been about eight because I'm older than Freddie. So you're going to say about a year younger than you? Not quite a year, but Freddie ought to be about 71 years old now. How old is that you're 72? And I'm 72. Now February the 2nd I'll be 73. February coming. Well I'll be 73 years old. Well about a month after that I'll be about 72. And of course I have my sister when she's old. She's like that much. Your wife mentioned that your sister's living here now. Yeah that's what I got back then. You said she'd be 79 in February? She'd be 79 in February. She'd be 79 in February. February the 15th. February the 15th she'd be 79. Does she remember much about the family? I wonder if she'd be able to give us an interview. Do you think she would mind it? Well I'll tell you.
I would like to do it. But of course now as the doctor gives her up and says look to you for her. I'll bring her home. She has a stroke. She's had a stroke. And uh well she had to bring her home.

She can't hardly explain her words. See and then a stroke makes her walk on her bed. And she'd have to drag her foot. So I had to bring her home from where she was living on St. Fella Street. 1827 St. Fella. So I brought her home. And I had to move all the things over here. As we had sufficient enough place to put it. Well of course my wife, she was the one that suggested to bring her home. Because people don't like to have trouble with you when you get so old, you get sicker. Somebody got to take care of you. So I just said, well, me and my wife got together and I brought her home. So that's where, well, we have plenty of trouble with her now. Don't say that.
